title: Capstone: A Fused Kernel
blurb: Tests why LayerNorm is a fusion target, the design of a one-load, one-store Triton kernel, verifying correctness and launch count, benchmarking against both a naive and a vendor baseline, and what torch.compile, F.layer_norm and the hand-written kernel each showed.

refLinks.label: §47.2.2 Design Decision 2: One Kernel, Three Loads, One Store
§47.2.1 Design Decision 1: Triton, Not Raw CUDA

questions.prompt: Why is the naive PyTorch LayerNorm slow?
options: Each step is a kernel that moves the whole tensor.
It uses Tensor Cores, which are slow for reductions.
It runs on the CPU unless the tensor is pinned.
It computes the variance in double precision.
questions.explanation: Mean, variance, subtract, divide and scale-and-shift each launch a kernel and move the whole tensor. A fused kernel reads x once and writes y once.

questions.prompt: Is LayerNorm memory-bound or compute-bound, and what does that imply?
options: Compute-bound, so the lever is faster arithmetic per element.
Memory-bound, so cut the bytes moved.
Compute-bound, so fusion will make little difference.
Neither, since reductions sit exactly on the ridge point.
questions.explanation: LayerNorm does a handful of FLOPs per element, far below the ridge. Every design choice in the kernel aims at reducing traffic.

refLinks.label: §47.2.2 Design Decision 2: One Kernel, Three Loads, One Store

questions.prompt: The design section is called "One Kernel, Three Loads, One Store". What are the three loads?
options: x three times, once each for mean, variance and output
x, the output buffer and epsilon
x, the weight and the bias
The mean, the variance and x
questions.explanation: x is loaded once per row and reused for mean, variance and normalising. The learnable weight and bias are the two small extra loads.

refLinks.label: §47.2.2 Design Decision 2: One Kernel, Three Loads, One Store

questions.prompt: Which conditions does Procedure 47.1 look for in a good fusion candidate? Select all that apply.
options: The ops share data
At least two ops in the sequence
Every op is memory-bound
Every op is compute-bound
questions.explanation: Fusion removes memory round trips between ops that share data. If an op is compute-bound, the heuristic says to check first, since fusion may not help.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't fusing two operations that share no data help?
options: Triton refuses to compile kernels with two independent outputs.
There's no round trip to remove.
The GPU can't hold two unrelated tensors in registers.
Independent operations always run faster as separate launches.
questions.explanation: Fusion's whole benefit is removing a redundant write and read between ops on the same data. Without that, there is nothing to save.

questions.prompt: Why was the capstone written in Triton?
options: Reduce-then-elementwise suits Triton's block model.
Raw CUDA can't express a row-wise reduction.
PyTorch only accepts custom ops written in Triton.
Triton kernels can't be beaten by vendor libraries.
questions.explanation: Chapter 44's softmax showed Triton matching PyTorch on this pattern. A Chapter 45 CUDA extension is a legitimate alternative.

options: Launching one program per column instead of per row
Computing the reduction in fp32 instead of fp16
Using a mask on the load, which slows the kernel
Loading x again for the elementwise step
questions.explanation: The loaded block can stay in registers between the reduction and the elementwise step. Reloading throws away much of what fusion gains.

questions.prompt: In Listing 47.2, masked-off columns load as other=0.0. Why is 0.0 safe for this mean, when softmax used -inf?
options: The mean uses tl.sum, and zeros add nothing to a sum divided by n_cols.
Masked lanes aren't included in tl.sum at all.
Zeros make the mean larger, which the normalisation step cancels out later.
0.0 is never safe. The kernel has a bug.
questions.explanation: Padding must be the identity for the reduction. For a sum that is 0, and the division uses n_cols, the real count. Softmax's max needs −∞. Masked lanes do take part in the reduction, which is why the value matters.

questions.prompt: Why was correctness checked before any timing?
options: Timing can't run until the correctness check has freed some GPU memory.
Triton requires a correctness check before benchmarking.
A fast kernel that is wrong is worse than a slow one that's right.
The check warms up the GPU for the benchmark.
questions.explanation: A speed claim without a correctness check isn't trustworthy. The kernel matched F.layer_norm to about 2.9e-6, float32 rounding.

questions.prompt: How does Procedure 47.3 confirm that a kernel really fused?
options: It counts kernel launches with torch.profiler.
It checks that the Python function has only one line.
It reads the kernel's source for a single @triton.jit.
It compares the output to F.layer_norm.
questions.explanation: Python structure doesn't prove launch count. The profiler shows what actually ran. That is also how torch.compile's single fused kernel was confirmed.

questions.prompt: The Triton output differed from F.layer_norm by at most about 2.9e-6. How should that be read?
options: As too small to measure, so the check is meaningless.
As proof the Triton kernel is more accurate.
As float32 rounding, not a bug in the formula.
As a bug, since correct kernels match exactly.
questions.explanation: Different reduction orders round differently in float32. An error at the 1e-6 level on values near 1 is expected. Chapter 45's exact 0.0 came from identical arithmetic.

options: Averaging over 50 repetitions
Running warm-up calls before timing
Comparing only against the naive version
Timing with CUDA events instead of time.perf_counter
questions.explanation: Beating a naive decomposition is easy and can mislead. A fusion claim needs both comparison points. The other three are the procedure's correct practice.

questions.prompt: In Listing 47.4, why is torch.cuda.synchronize() called after the warm-up loop?
options: So warm-up work finishes before timing starts
So the warm-up results are copied to the host
So the GPU clock speed resets to its base value
It isn't needed, since events are synchronous
questions.explanation: Launches are asynchronous. Without the sync, leftover warm-up work could fall inside the timed window.

questions.prompt: How many kernel launches did the naive PyTorch LayerNorm make?
questions.explanation: The naive version launched 7 kernels. torch.compile, F.layer_norm and the Triton kernel each launched 1.

questions.prompt: The naive version took about 0.121 ms and torch.compile about 0.036 ms. What is the speedup? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 0.121 / 0.036 = 3.36, from a one-line change. The chapter calls torch.compile the cheapest first resort.

questions.prompt: torch.compile fused the naive LayerNorm into one kernel, yet it still trailed F.layer_norm by 1.7x. Why?
options: It ran in double precision.
It skipped the correctness check.
Its general heuristics missed a specialised reduction.
It launched seven kernels, not one.
questions.explanation: One launch isn't the whole story. How the reduction inside is organised matters too. That gap is why hand-written kernels remain a live skill.

questions.prompt: The hand-written kernel (about 0.018 ms) beat F.layer_norm (about 0.021 ms). What does the chapter say this does and doesn't show?
options: F.layer_norm is badly written and should be avoided.
The result is noise, since a 3 µs gap can't be measured.
A real result for this shape, not a general rule.
Hand-written kernels are generally faster than vendor libraries.
questions.explanation: A kernel built for one shape can out-specialise a library that must handle many shapes, dtypes and edge cases. The chapter warns against generalising, and points to the book's null results too.

bookExercises.prompt: Write LayerNorm's formula and state how many separate operations a naive PyTorch decomposition requires versus a fused kernel.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `y = (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + eps) * weight + bias`. A naive PyTorch decomposition requires 7 separate operations/kernel launches (confirmed via `torch.profiler`); a fused kernel computes the same result in 1 launch.

bookExercises.prompt: State Procedure 47.4's rule about what a fusion benchmark must always compare against, and explain in one sentence why comparing only to the naive version is a weaker claim.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A fusion benchmark must always compare against both the naive/decomposed version AND the best available vendor implementation, if one exists. Comparing only to the naive version is a weaker claim because it only shows "better than the worst case." It says nothing about whether the new kernel is actually competitive with what's already available off the shelf, which is the comparison that actually matters for deciding whether custom kernel work was worthwhile.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's measured table (naive 0.121 ms, vendor 0.021 ms, capstone kernel 0.018 ms), compute the speedup of the capstone kernel over the naive decomposition AND over the vendor implementation separately, and explain why reporting only the first number would understate the more impressive claim.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Speedup over naive: `0.118 / 0.016 ≈ 7.4x`. Speedup over the vendor implementation: `0.021 / 0.016 ≈ 1.3x`. Reporting only the naive-comparison number (7.4x) would understate the more impressive and harder-to-achieve claim. Beating a vendor-optimised, heavily-engineered general-purpose implementation by any margin (here roughly 31% faster) is a much stronger result than beating an unoptimized 7-kernel decomposition, since the vendor baseline already captures most of the "obvious" optimization headroom.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 47.5's measured correctness result (~2.9e-6 max absolute error), explain what magnitude of error would have indicated a genuine formula bug rather than float32 rounding, and why "the kernel is 7x faster" would not be a trustworthy claim without this check having passed first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A max absolute error meaningfully larger than float32's expected rounding-error range (roughly 1e-6 to 1e-5 for operations of this complexity), for example an error in the 1e-2 or larger range, or an error that grows with input magnitude in a way inconsistent with simple rounding, would indicate a genuine formula bug (e.g. a single-pass vs. two-pass variance formula difference, or an off-by-one in the reduction) rather than floating-point noise. Without this check passing first, "the kernel is 7x faster" would not be trustworthy because a kernel could be fast specifically because it's doing less work than the correct formula requires. Speed and correctness are independent claims, and a wrong-but-fast kernel is worse than a correct-but-slow one, since its wrong answer would silently propagate downstream.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague wants to fuse two operations in their pipeline: a matrix multiply followed immediately by a lookup into a large embedding table with no relationship to the matmul's output. Using Procedure 47.1's heuristic, explain why this is likely a poor fusion candidate.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Per Procedure 47.1's heuristic, the second condition (`shares_data = True`) fails here: the embedding lookup doesn't read the matmul's output or share any memory traffic with it. The two operations are only sequential in the pipeline, not data-dependent on each other in a way fusion could exploit. Fusing them would combine unrelated work into one kernel without eliminating any redundant read/write, adding code complexity for no bandwidth benefit, exactly the "common mistake" the procedure warns against.

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 47.3 warns that a "one Python function call" can hide multiple kernel launches. Describe a concrete scenario, using this chapter's discussion of dtype handling, where a kernel that looks fused in source code would fail Procedure 47.3's verification check.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If a "fused" wrapper function checks the input dtype and falls back to a separate, unfused PyTorch implementation for an unsupported dtype (e.g. the Triton kernel only handles fp32/fp16 but the wrapper silently calls `torch.nn.functional.layer_norm` for fp64 inputs), the Python source looks like a single fused call in every case, but `torch.profiler` would show more than one kernel signature when that fallback path is exercised. The "one Python function call" appearance hides a conditional branch that isn't actually fused for every input.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the official Triton "Layer Normalization" tutorial's backward-pass implementation. Identify one additional complexity the backward pass introduces that the forward pass in this chapter's Procedure 47.2 doesn't need to handle.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The backward pass for a reduction-then-elementwise operation like LayerNorm needs gradients with respect to both the input AND the learnable `weight`/`bias` parameters, and because the forward pass's mean/variance depend on every element in the row, the backward pass's gradient for any single input element also depends on every other element in that same row. This requires a second, more complex reduction (summing gradient contributions across the row) that the forward pass, which only needs one reduction to compute the shared mean/variance, doesn't need to handle.
